ov: Sea animals that live as colonies of many identical polyps, each a few millimetres across with a ring of stinging tentacles around its mouth. Reef-building corals lay down a hard limestone skeleton and build reefs such as the Great Barrier Reef; other corals live in cold, deep water.

why.d: Its polyps catch plankton and small fish with stinging tentacles, but most reef corals get most of their energy from algae living inside their tissues.
why.ac: Most corals pull their tentacles in by day and spread them at night to catch plankton.

rg: Tropical and subtropical reefs, mostly in clear water less than 60 m deep; cold-water corals live as deep as 3,300 m and as far north as Scotland and the Aleutian Islands.
df: Plankton and small fish caught with stinging tentacles, plus food made by the algae living in its tissues.
fx: People thought corals were plants until the 18th century, when William Herschel saw under a microscope that they are animals.
Many corals spawn all at once overnight, often around a full moon.
